Give reasons. 12.5 Determination of Thermal Conductivity of Good Conductor; Searle's Method The coefficient of thermal conductivity of a body is defined as the amount of heat flowing per second at a steady state across the opposite faces of a unit cube maintained at unit temperature difference. The thermal conductivity of a conducting solid in the form of a rod can be determined by Searle's method in the laboratory from the setup as shown in figure 12.5.
Suppose, there is a metal rod AB whose thermal conductivity (k) is to be determined. Except for cross-section at A and B, the whole rod is kept inside an insulated box to prevent any loss

of heat from its sides. The rod taken has a uniform cross-section (say A) and it has two cavities P and Q at a distance x apart as in figure 12.5. Thermometers T1 and T2 respectively are inserted in cavities P and Q. The cavities P and Q are filled with mercury so that accurate measurement of the temperature can be achieved. Also, steam is circulated continuously at end A whereas a cooling pipe of copper is wound near end B, and cold water is circulated continuously through it. The flowing water absorbs heat from the rod, and becomes warm. The warm water is collected into a vessel. Two thermometers, T4 and T3 are used to measure the temperature of cold water used, and warm water collected in the vessel respectively. The mass of water collected for a given time is measured. Let t be the time for which heat flows from point P to Q to reach to a steady state.
After the circulation of steam, the temperature readings on thermometer T1, T2 and T3 increase
continuously. When a steady state of heating is achieved, the rate of heat flow through any
cross-section of the rod is the same, and all the thermometers show a constant temperature
